author: Billy Arnold / Managing Editor
title: Rain, changing weather pattern to dissipate Teton County's unhealthy wildfire smoke | Environmental | jhnewsandguide.com
text:
With rainstorms set to move through the valley today and Thursday, unhealthy smoke that blanketed Jackson Hole is expected to clear.
The haze enveloping the valley is a reminder of how difficult wildfire smoke can make breathing for people sensitive to air pollution — and Jacksonites accustomed to getting outside before or after work.
“That’s the rule of thumb: If you can see it and smell it, it’s OK to not exercise,” said Jim Woodmencey, a meteorologist and News&Guide columnist who also runs Mountain Weather, a Jackson Hole weather site.
“If you can smell it, you should probably back off on the rigorousness of your exercise,” Woodmencey added. “But if you can taste it, you really shouldn’t be exercising outside.”
Overnight Monday, smoke could be smelled through open windows and, at first light Tuesday, tasted. Blowing north from the Dollar Fire near Green River Lakes, as well as east from fires in Idaho, the smoke caused air quality to deteriorate throughout western Wyoming.
At 9 a.m. Tuesday, the air quality index for small particulate matter in Alta was hovering around 153, which the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency considers “unhealthy” for everyone.
At that level, the EPA recommends sensitive people “avoid long or intense outdoor activities” and “consider rescheduling or moving activities indoors.” For everyone else, the agency recommends people “reduce long or intense activities” and “take more breaks during outdoor activities.”
By press time Tuesday, the index in Alta had fallen to roughly 85, which the EPA considers “moderate” air quality. At that level, the EPA says unusually sensitive groups may notice symptoms, such as coughing or shortness of breath. For everyone else, the agency says it’s a “good day to be outside.”
Smoke lingered longer on the east side of the Tetons. In Moose, the day started with an air quality index of 163. That climbed to a peak of 178 by noon, and then trailed off to roughly 155 by press time Tuesday.
All of those levels are considered “unhealthy.”
Teton County health officials say everyone should consider avoiding “prolonged outdoor exercise” when the air quality index exceeds 200. They also say at-risk people should limit smoke exposure. That includes people with pre-existing heart and lung conditions, older people who are at risk of those conditions, and children, whose respiratory systems are still developing.
Smoke should dissipate today as rain moves in, Woodmencey said. As a more southwesterly flow hits the region later this week, the wind should blow smoke east, away from Jackson and Pinedale.
